activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Egyptians used nilometers, stairs or pillars marked with measurements beside the river, to track how high the Nile flood rose and predict the size of the harvest.
story:
Zoe sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her poster board, a marker with a dying tip, and a problem. Tomorrow she had to explain to her class why the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming, and all she had so far was a title and one sparse paragraph copied from a website. The rest of the page was blank. She pressed her palm against it, as if pressure might push ideas out of the paper.

Carlos arrived after dinner with his notebook and a bag of pretzels. "I found something at the museum last month," he said, flipping pages. "There was this stairway going down into water, with carved lines on the steps, like ruler marks. I stood there forever trying to figure it out." He tapped his drawing. "Then it clicked. They were measuring how high the river rose. It's called a nilometer."

Zoe grabbed a glass from her desk and set it in the bathtub her little brother had left half full. "Okay, pretend this is the Nile," she said, crouching beside the tub. She drew a small mark on the glass at the waterline, then dumped in a cup of water. The line climbed. "Every year the flood came up, and the marks on the stairs or pillars beside the river told them exactly how high it got." She poured another cup and watched the level rise past the second mark. "So a good flood meant a big harvest, and a low one meant trouble. They could predict it before a single seed went in the ground."

"That's the perspective you were missing," Carlos said through a mouthful of pretzels. "The pyramids, the farms, all of it, it runs on the river." Zoe wrote across the top of her poster, then underlined it twice. "Tomorrow I'm going to summarize the whole thing in one sentence," she said, "but first I need to draw stairs going down into water." She picked up the dying marker and shook it, and it came back to life.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Jordan counted the finished posters leaning against the gym wall and came up one short. The Heritage Showcase was Friday, and his club was supposed to have twelve displays, one for every member. His own poster, about northern communities, sat half-finished on the long table because he couldn't get the caption right. He had written "An Inuit hunter builds a snow house" and then crossed out "An," then written it again, then crossed it out so many times the paper had gone grey and soft.

Avril leaned over his shoulder. "You're going to wear a hole through it."

"It sounds wrong," Jordan said. "The whole sentence. But I don't know what part is wrong."

Kallie spun a chair around and sat on it backward. "Then ask Mr. Toussaint. He's got that whole shelf of books by the door."

Jordan didn't want to ask. He wanted to figure it out himself, the way he figured out the club's poster schedule when everyone's names got mixed up. He went to the shelf anyway and pulled down a book about the Arctic. He found a picture of a single man in a parka, and the label under it. The word there wasn't the one he'd written. He flipped to another page, then another, and a pattern showed up, like the median on the graph in math class, one steady thing in the middle of everything else. One page showed a group, and the other word showed a person.

He grabbed a sticky note and wrote himself a message, then read it to Avril:

"Dear Jordan. Stop crossing out words with your whole arm. The problem is one letter. You're welcome. Sincerely, also Jordan."

Avril laughed so hard Mr. Toussaint came over. Jordan held up the book, pointing at the picture of the one man. "It says Inuk," he said. "One person is an Inuk. Inuit means 'the people.'" He looked at the group photo on the next page, then at his own poster. "I had it backwards."

Mr. Toussaint nodded but didn't take over, which Jordan appreciated. The change would be gradual, though, because the poster still needed its map, and its timeline, and half a border of paper snowflakes by Thursday.

"You'll make the deadline," Avril said, trying to reassure him. "You have the hard part done. The one-letter part."

Jordan copied the new caption in careful letters: "An Inuk hunter builds a snow house." Then he taped his sticky note to the corner of the poster, where everyone at the showcase could see it.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: The phrase "according to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist.
story:
The argument had already sustained itself for ten minutes of practice, which was ten minutes nobody had spent actually playing. Michelle said her goal counted because the ball had touched the cone before rolling wide. Emy said a cone was not a goalpost, no matter what it touched, and that anyone who thought otherwise was inventing rules on the spot.

Alexandra stood between them on the chalk line the coach had drawn across the gym floor like an equator, one team's half on each side. She was wondering something else entirely. Michelle wasn't cheating, exactly. She was playing by a rule she truly believed existed, and so was Emy, and the two rules were not equivalent. The problem wasn't either of them. The problem was that nobody had ever written the rule down.

"Wait," Alexandra said. "Before we fight more. What's the actual rule about cones?"

"Cones are the goal," said Michelle.

"Cones are just cones," said Emy.

"See? That's the problem," Alexandra said. "Not the shot. Nobody ever agreed what a cone is. My grandpa plays cards with a rulebook so old it has a name for this."

That night she found the note her grandpa had tucked into her duffel bag after his last visit, folded into a small square. She smoothed it out on her desk and read it again: "When I come at the end of the month, we play whist, and we play it properly, according to Hoyle." Underneath he had drawn a tiny mustachioed face with a question mark. Alexandra had laughed the first time she read it, and she laughed again now, because she still had no idea who Hoyle was. She looked it up, and the answer was better than she'd guessed. "According to Hoyle" means following the rules exactly; it comes from Edmond Hoyle, whose 1742 book set down the rules of the card game whist. A man so serious about rules that people were still quoting him nearly three hundred years later, usually while pointing a finger.

At practice the next day, Alexandra raised her hand like she was in class, which made Michelle snort milk out of her nose from her water bottle, which made even Emy laugh. "New plan," Alexandra said. "We name the problem out loud, then we make one rule everyone agrees on before we play. That's the Hoyle way."

"Who's Hoyle?" Emy asked.

"Some old card player. He wrote the rules down so nobody had to fight about them."

"So cones are... what, exactly?" Michelle asked.

"Officially out," Alexandra said. "Unless both captains agree before the game that they count. That's the fair version."

Michelle stuck out her hand. Emy shook it, then immediately yelled, "Okay, but if she scores off a cone again, I'm writing to this Hoyle guy myself."

"Good luck," Alexandra said. "You'll need a really old envelope."

Emy positioned the ball at the chalk line, Michelle crouched into her stance, and the game finally began.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food banks usually rotate stock by 'first in, first out', sending older items out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves.
story:
Kaitlyn stacked the last box of soup cans at the front of the shelf, right where the labels could be seen, and stepped back to admire her work. The whole row looked neat, all the new stock lined up like soldiers.

"You did that fast," said Layan, who was sorting pasta two shelves over. Kayson was behind them, taping a ripped cereal box, and Mr. Quinn, the volunteer coordinator, came around the corner with his clipboard and stopped so abruptly that his shoes squeaked on the concrete floor.

He pulled a can from the front of Kaitlyn's shelf and turned it over in his hand. "Where did these come from?"

"The delivery this morning," Kaitlyn said. "I put the new ones in front because the labels are nicer."

Mr. Quinn held up an older can from the back, its paper label worn soft at the edges, almost eroded away by years of being picked up and put down. "These older ones have to go out first. First in, first out."

Kaitlyn frowned. "But the new ones look better."

"That's what Kayson said last week," Layan offered, and Kayson groaned from behind the cereal boxes.

Kaitlyn looked at the two cans side by side and thought about it. The old can had a date stamped on the bottom, closer than the date on the new one. If the new cans went out the door today, the old ones would sit there, growing older on the shelf, until nobody could use them at all. She tested her idea by checking three more pairs from different shelves. Every time, the front can in Mr. Quinn's system had the closest date, and the new stock waited behind it.

"So the shelf is kind of a line," she said. "The cans at the front are next to leave."

"Exactly like a queue," Mr. Quinn said, and moved on to the next aisle.

Kaitlyn pulled the new cans forward in her arms and restacked everything, older ones in front, newer ones behind. It took twice as long as the first time, and Layan came over to help without being asked, sliding cans down to her one at a time.

A woman with a small boy on her hip came through the line near closing. Kaitlyn handed her one of the old-front cans, and the woman read the label and smiled. "Split pea. My mom's favorite."

Kaitlyn watched the can go into the woman's bag, first in line, first out the door.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers, and the animals that eat them are called secondary consumers.
story:
Felix crouched at the edge of Miller's Pond with his sketchbook open and a pencil that had been sharpened down to a stub. His problem was due tomorrow: a science project showing a food chain, drawn from the sun all the way to a top predator, with an explanation of what would happen if one link disappeared. He had never drawn anything for science before, and the blank page felt like it was daring him.

Kaila dropped onto the grass beside him, holding a bag of sunflower seeds. "You've been staring at that paper for ten minutes," she said. "The sun's not going to hop onto it by itself."

"I know it starts with the sun," Felix said. "Then the pond plants, because they grow using sunlight. Then something eats the plants." He pointed at a cluster of green stems poking out of the shallow water. "Snails, maybe. And then something eats the snails. A bird? Mr. Wiśniewski said we have herons here."

Bentley jogged up with his sneakers squelching. "I counted four herons on the far bank yesterday," he reported. "Also about a million tadpoles, and I saw a water beetle grab a tadpole. It was intense."

Felix started sketching fast: sun, plants, snails. Then he stopped, pencil hovering. "Wait. The heron is my top predator. It eats the water beetles, right? Or the snails? I can't just guess. I have to get the order right, or the whole explanation falls apart."

"Think about who eats what," Kaila said, cracking a seed between her teeth. "The snails only eat the plants. The beetles eat the snails and the tadpoles."

Felix sat back. "My dad said animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers," he said slowly, watching a snail slide along a stem. "So the snails are the primary consumers. And the animals that eat them are secondary consumers. The beetles. Then the heron eats the beetles, so it's next up the chain."

"That tracks," said Bentley. "So draw it: sun, plants, snails, beetle, heron. Five links."

Felix drew each link as a circle connected by arrows, and labeled them. Then Kaila leaned over his shoulder and frowned. "Okay, but you still have to explain what happens if one link disappears. Pick one."

"Testing time," Felix announced. He held his thumb over the beetle circle. "If the beetles vanish, the herons lose a big food source. But the snails would go nuts with nothing eating them, so they'd eat way more plants, and the plants would shrink, and then the snails would run out of food too." He slid his thumb over the snail circle instead. "And if the snails disappear, the beetles get hungry and the plants overgrow the whole pond." He looked up. "Take out any link and both sides of it get messed up."

Kaila raised her seed bag as if toasting him. "The pond has spoken, and I think we have a consensus."

"Rain's imminent," Bentley said, pointing at a gray bank of cloud rolling in over the far trees. "Draw faster."

Felix added one last detail, a heron standing in the shallows with its neck curved like a question mark, and printed his name at the bottom of the page just as the first fat drops hit the water.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Obsidian is volcanic glass: lava that cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form.
story:
Kayla spread the rocks across the picnic table in her backyard, sorting them into three rows: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic. Her ambition was to beat Sulaiman in Monday's geology quiz, and she had promised Katia a slice of lemon cake if Katia gave up her Saturday to help.

Katia held up a shiny black rock that caught the sun like a mirror. "This one's easy. Somebody melted a glass bottle and it got all over the beach."

"It's a rock," Kayla said, frowning. But when she looked closer, it did look exactly like glass, with a curved edge sharp enough to slice paper. She turned it over in her fingers. It was cold and smooth, with no sparkles inside, while the granite beside it glittered with tiny crystals. That difference had to mean something.

She ran her thumb across the granite's speckles. Crystals everywhere. Then she rubbed the black rock again. Nothing. She remembered Ms. Huang saying rocks told stories about how they formed, if you knew how to read them. Igneous meant cooled lava. So the crystals in granite had somehow had time to grow, and the black rock had not. She had a simple idea. "I think this is lava that cooled so fast the crystals didn't have time to form," she said slowly. "Cooling fast would make it smooth like glass. Volcanic glass."

Katia leaned over the fence and called to Ms. Huang, who was watering her tomatoes next door. Ms. Huang set down the hose and came over, wiping her hands on her shorts. "Let me see that." She held it up to the light, turned it, then handed it back. "That's obsidian. Volcanic glass. Lava that cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form."

Kayla pumped her fist. Then she felt her cheeks go warm, because Katia was still holding the glass-bottle theory like a defiant shield. "I was sure," Katia admitted.

"That's okay. I got the sedimentary and metamorphic ones backwards all last week," Kayla confessed. "Put the obsidian in the igneous row, and I'll cut the cake."

Katia placed it next to the pumice, then stuck her finger against the sharp edge and yelped. Kayla fetched a bandage from the kitchen drawer and pressed it gently around her friend's finger. "Volcanic glass cuts," she said. "Now you'll never forget what it is."

Katia grinned and picked up the lemon cake slice with her good hand. Kayla wrote OBSIDIAN in careful letters on her chart, then set the shiny black rock on top of the granite, where it gleamed like a small black mirror in the afternoon sun.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Wyatt slumped in the desk chair and clicked on the group chat for his science project. Mattea and Karissa had been messaging all afternoon while he was at his grandma's, and the messages had accelerated since the last time he checked, filling two whole screens. They had chosen the topic without him. Volcanoes. His idea about consumer packaging waste was gone, voted out in a poll he never saw.

He wanted them to notice him. He wanted to matter in this chat. So he typed fast and hit enter.

"WHERE ARE YOU"

Three dots appeared under Mattea's name. Then they vanished. Then they came back.

"why are you yelling?" Karissa wrote.

Wyatt stared at the screen. Yelling? His house was quiet except for the fan humming in the corner and the sticky sound of his chair when he shifted. He had typed the same letters he always typed, just bigger.

"I wasn't yelling," he wrote back, and then, because that felt flat, he added, "why did it look like yelling?"

Mattea answered first. "all caps reads as shouting. everybody knows that."

Karissa sent a shrugging emoji. "you sounded mad at us."

He wasn't mad, exactly. He felt like the last kid picked for a team, standing at the edge of the field. He had been pessimistic about the project all week, and now the chat seemed to prove him right. He decided to test it, though, because Mattea's claim sounded like a rule, and rules could be checked.

He typed, "OKAY, I WILL BRING THE MARKERS TOMORROW."

"still yelling," Karissa replied instantly.

Then he typed it again, small letters, easy: "okay, i will bring the markers tomorrow."

"see? better," Mattea wrote. "also we can still talk about packaging. mr. farah-ali said we could compare volcano damage to plastic waste if we split the poster in half."

Wyatt leaned forward so fast the chair creaked. He wrote, "I can do the packaging side. I already have a pile of wrappers in my closet for evidence." He looked at the capital I and decided one letter was fine.

"deal," Mattea sent. "bring the wrappers."

Wyatt got up, pulled the shoebox of crinkled chip bags and yogurt cups from under his bed, and set it beside the keyboard for morning.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
story:
Lincoln had been at Grandpa's house since noon, along with Alexandre and Quinn, because the championship was starting at two and Grandpa had the biggest television on the block. The plan had almost been thwarted when the screen went dark an hour before kickoff, and Grandpa had spent ten minutes hunting for the receipt to check whether the TV was still under warranty. It was not. But then Mr. Wijaya, the neighbor, appeared at the door holding a remote that looked equivalent to the lost one, pressed three buttons, and the picture came back, and everyone cheered as if the game had already been won.

By the fourth quarter, the home team was ahead by three, and Alexandre was pacing behind the couch. "They're only winning because they're at home," he said. "Put this game in the other team's stadium and it flips. Watch."

"That's not a real thing," Quinn said, mouth full of popcorn. "That's just something people say when their team loses."

Lincoln thought about it. He did not say anything at first, because a claim like that could be checked, and checking was better than arguing. He pulled out his phone and started looking up season records, keeping one eye on the screen where the home team was driving down the field. He wrote numbers on the back of Grandpa's TV guide: wins at home, wins on the road, sport by sport.

"Okay," he said during a timeout. "Look. In basketball, football, hockey, baseball, most major sports, the home teams win more than half their games. It's a real pattern, not a feeling. It even has a name. Home advantage."

Alexandre threw both fists in the air, as though he had just scored himself. "Thank you. Home advantage."

Quinn leaned over the list of numbers. His shoulders dropped a little. "That's a lot of seasons," he admitted. "Fine, it's real. I was wrong." Then he squinted at the paper. "But more than half isn't everything. Away teams still win a lot."

Lincoln had been thinking the same thing. If home advantage was real, then the pattern should show up somewhere you could test it. He turned to Grandpa. "Do you still have that binder with all the old standings?"

Grandpa did, in the basement, going back thirty years. Lincoln and Quinn ran down while Alexandre guarded the couch, and they pulled five random seasons, added up home wins and road wins, and the home wins were ahead every single time, by more than half.

Upstairs, the home team kicked the winning field goal, and Alexandre screamed so loudly that Mr. Wijaya knocked on the wall from next door. Quinn looked at the binder still open on the coffee table, then at the celebrating screen.

"Next week they play away," he said. "I still think they win."

"Then you're saying home advantage isn't everything," Lincoln said, and handed him the popcorn.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience.
story:
Andrew stood on the coffee table in the living room, facing the couch, the way Ms. Dang had told the choir to face the audience. On Friday, three days from now, he would sing in his first concert, and the note she had handed out said the whole choir must "exit stage left." The trouble was, he had no idea which side that was, and neither did Simon or Cullen, who were sprawled on the couch pretending to be a crowd.

"It's obvious," Simon said, pointing at the window. "Left is left. We go that way."

Cullen frowned. "But Ms. Dang said stage left from her spot in the wings, and she's on the other side."

Andrew jumped down and tried an experiment. He made his little brother's toy plane, the one with the spinning propeller, stand on the coffee table facing the couch, just like a performer facing an audience. Then he walked around behind it, pretending to be Ms. Dang looking out from the wings. From behind the plane, its left wing pointed toward the window, which was Simon's left too, but wait. He crouched to the plane's side, where its left wing would be if the plane were a person, and it pointed at the bookshelf. The two directions were opposite. "Stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience," he said slowly, testing each word. "So we go toward the bookshelf side. Our own left."

Simon looked doubtful until they practiced. Cullen called out "Exit stage left!" and Simon spun toward the window, then caught himself, laughed, and crossed to the bookshelf side instead. They drilled it four more times, until nobody hesitated. Even the spontaneous round of applause they gave themselves, led by Cullen pounding the couch cushions, couldn't distract them.

The night of the concert, Andrew's stomach flipped as the curtains opened, and his first note came out thin. But when the final song ended, Ms. Dang raised her hand toward the bookshelf side of the stage, and every choir member turned left together, clean and sure. From the dark rows of seats, a single loud whistle cut through the applause, and Andrew knew it by its pitch.

"That's my dad," he whispered to Simon as they walked off.

activity: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
knowledge_domain: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
fact: A sound's pitch depends on its frequency, the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz; faster vibrations make a higher pitch.
story:
Christopher stood at the top of the half-pipe with his board under his feet, and his whole body said no. Below him, Zaiden and Brinley waited on the flat concrete, and the drop looked about ten times steeper than it had from the ground.

"You're overthinking it," Zaiden called up. "Just commit."

Christopher crouched, rolled his weight forward, and bailed almost instantly, sliding down on his knees while the board rattled away behind him. When he chased it down, the wheels were still buzzing against the pavement. He picked it up and felt the hum in the deck with his fingertips.

"Sound is just that," Brinley said, tapping the board. "Vibrations travelling through stuff. Air, concrete, water, whatever."

Zaiden sat on the bench nearby and pressed a steel ruler against the edge, flicking the overhanging part so it went brrrrr. Then he slid it shorter and flicked again, and the note climbed higher. "Frequency," he said. "The number of vibrations per second. It's measured in hertz." He flicked a tiny stub of ruler sticking out and got a thin, high buzz. "Faster vibrations, higher pitch."

"Say that again," Christopher said, still holding his humming board.

"Vibrations per second. Hertz," Zaiden said. "Fewer per second, low note. More, high note."

Brinley had pulled out her phone. "Ms. Abdi told us sound goes way faster through water than air. That's why whales hear each other across whole bays."

"That sounds controversial," Zaiden said.

"It's not, it's real. She showed us a video where a whale call travels like a rumour through a whole harbour. And this other one about a microbe that swims toward sound, which, honestly, felt made up."

Christopher set his board down, spun the wheel with his thumb, and felt the vibration tick against his finger, faster than the big slow wobble of the deck when he bounced on it. Fast ticks, high squeak. Slow wobble, low drone. He grinned.

He carried the board back up to the top of the ramp, set the tail on the coping, and breathed in. He thought of the short ruler, the quick buzz, the way a small fast thing could carry a whole clear note.

"Watch this," he called down, and rolled in.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
Ivy pulled the kitchen chair up to the family computer and typed the address Kelly-Ann had written on a scrap of paper. The site was called BugBook, and Kelly-Ann and Aida both had accounts already. They had spent all of recess trading beetle stickers on it, and Ivy wanted in before the good ones were gone. She clicked "Create Account," picked a username, and then the form asked for her birthday.

She typed it honestly: March 14. The screen went red. "You must be 13 or older to create a BugBook account." Ivy sat back. Kelly-Ann was eleven, just like her, and Aida was still ten until June. So how did they have accounts? She tried a test. She made a new username, typed every answer exactly the same, except the year, which she changed so the site would think she was fourteen. This time the screen said, "Ask a parent for permission before continuing." The site had a parent-permission option, but only when it believed you were over thirteen.

In the hall above her, Dad was unrolling pink insulation into the attic floor, and the thumping came right through the ceiling. She carried the laptop up the ladder and showed him the permission screen. "Can you do this?" she asked. Dad read it, then scrolled down to a link that said "Why do you need my birthday?" Ivy leaned in and read it out loud: "The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13. That is why many sites require users to be 13."

"So that's it," Ivy said. "The site isn't trying to keep kids out for fun. It's a law about collecting information." Dad negotiated with her for a while: she could have the account if he signed the consent form and she used only her first name, never her school, never her address. Ivy agreed to everything, then sat at the top of the ladder typing while Dad stapled insulation around the vent. She filled out the consent form the way a diligent student fills out a test, checking each box twice before clicking submit.

The account opened with a cheerful chirp. Aida's beetle sticker collection appeared on Ivy's screen, all forty of them, including the rare gold one. Ivy clicked "send trade request" and typed a message. "Hi! It's Ivy. Can I have the green one?" She waited, listening to the stapler thump above her, until the reply popped up. "Took you long enough," Aida wrote. "Deal."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Many persuasive essays end with a call to action, a sentence telling the reader exactly what they should do next.
story:
Natalie sat at the corner table in the library, where writing club met every Thursday after school. Her draft lay in front of her, four paragraphs about saving Miller Park from being turned into a parking lot. Ms. Owusu had said a persuasive essay needed five paragraphs, an introduction and a conclusion, and Natalie had counted hers three times. Four. Something was missing, but she could not see what, so she stared at the empty space after her last sentence.

Imran leaned over from the next chair. "You're stuck on the ending, aren't you. Charles-Edouard finished his in ten minutes." Across the table, Charles-Edouard was writing fast, which was annoying but also a clue. If he had finished quickly, maybe there was a pattern she could copy. She read his conclusion upside down. It ended with a direct order: "Sign the petition at the library desk." Natalie sat back. Every strong essay she could remember did something like that. Hers just stopped, like a door left half open.

She wrote one more sentence at the bottom of her page. Then she wrote a note and slid it across to Imran, because Ms. Owonu liked the room quiet during drafting time. "Mine ends by telling readers to sign the petition to preserve the park. Does that count as a real conclusion, or just a demand?" Imran read it, grinned, and wrote back: "It counts. Ms. Owusu calls that a call to action. It tells the reader exactly what to do next."

When the timer rang, Ms. Owusu walked the room and paused at Natalie's page. "Five paragraphs," she said. "Your argument stayed objective until the end, and then you gave your reader a job. Well done." She handed back the draft with a small check mark. Natalie read her last line again, then copied it onto a clean sheet, nice and neat, so the librarian could pin it by the petition forms. "Sign your name today," it said. "Miller Park needs fifty more people."

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: Unpaid search results are called organic results, and Google says advertisers cannot pay to move their pages higher in them.
story:
The office smelled like coffee and printer ink, and Avery had a whole hour to kill while her mom finished a meeting down the hall. She was supposed to be finding a science project topic, but every search she typed gave her a swamp of junk.

At the desk beside hers, Mattias leaned over from the visitor chair, chewing a straw he'd taken from the break room. "Just search 'best water filter,'" he said. "Whatever's on top is the winner, obviously."

Avery typed it. The very first result was a slick site called PureFlow, all glossy photos and a big orange button that said BUY NOW. "See?" Mattias said. "They must have paid Google a ton to sit up there. Number one spot, right? Nobody gets that for free."

Something about it bugged her, though. She scrolled back to the top and looked more carefully. Above PureFlow, in tiny grey letters, sat a small box she'd never once noticed before: the word "Sponsored." Below it, other links wore the same little label, like name tags at a party.

"Those are ads," she said slowly. "The ones without the tag are different." She clicked a help page and read fast, then read it again, because it seemed too weird. "Listen to this. The unpaid ones are called organic results. And Google says advertisers can't pay to move their pages higher in them." She deviseda quick test: search three other things, filter out anything marked Sponsored, and see whether the top organic results were the big famous sites or the loud shopping ones.

They ran it together. Each time, the ads crowded the top like shouting vendors, and just under them, the organic results led to library pages, university sites, and one surprisingly good contemporary science blog. PureFlow didn't appear in any of them.

Mattias dropped his straw in the trash. "So the top ad paid to be there, but the top real one earned it."

"Exactly." Avery copied three keywords into her notebook, folding the page so she wouldn't lose them. "Now, real search: 'science project, water quality, student.'" She hit Enter and leaned in as the results loaded.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
Romy spread her graph paper across the folding table in Grandma's basement, where the whole family had gathered for the reunion. Her homework was due Monday: a bar graph of the ethnic and cultural origins of a town in Canada, using real census numbers. She had copied the numbers carefully at school, but something was wrong. Scottish, 32 percent. English, 28 percent. French, 22 percent. Indian, Punjabi, Chinese, Ukrainian, six percent here, four percent there. She added them three times, and every time the total climbed past 130 percent.

"Your graph's broken," said Abbas, her cousin's friend, who had come along because he lived next door. He leaned over her shoulder and pointed at the column of numbers. "Percents can't do that. A hundred is all there is."

Romy didn't argue. She went upstairs to retrieve her notebook, where she had written the source of the numbers, and checked each bar against her notes. Everything was consistent: the same figures, the same town, the same year. The problem wasn't her copying.

"Maybe the census people made a mistake," Zac offered. He was Abbas's little brother, and he was eating a samosa while he talked. "Grown-ups mess stuff up all the time."

Romy considered that premise and rejected it. A national count that millions of people filled out would not be off by thirty percent. Someone would have noticed. She looked around the crowded basement, at her aunts and uncles arguing about cricket, at the table of food where jollof rice sat next to pierogi, and something clicked. "Zac," she said, "what are you?"

"Canadian and Jamaican," he said, like it was obvious.

"And you?" she asked Abbas.

"Pakistani and, well, Canadian. And my mom says Scottish too, from her grandmother."

Romy wrote both names on a napkin and drew a line under each. "So if a form asked your origins, you'd write down more than one thing." She counted on her fingers. "You'd get counted in two or three columns, but you're still one person. One person, three tallies." That was the hidden rule, and it explained everything: the town's totals could stack past one hundred without anyone lying and without anyone being counted twice as a person.

Her grandmother, passing through with a tray of cups, glanced at the napkin. "Since 1981 the census has let people report more than one origin," she said, setting down a cup of tea beside Romy's elbow. "That's why the totals add up to more than the whole population." Then she went back to the kitchen.

At the bottom of her graph, Romy printed a note: origins add to over 100 percent because people can report more than one. She taped the graph to the basement door and stood back. Abbas squinted at it, then at the napkin, then at his samosa. "So in a town like that," he said slowly, "almost everybody's a walking double bar."

Georgia slid her Spanish folder between the napkin dispenser and the ketchup bottle so Jared couldn't see her notes. "Mr. Greco said our family descriptions have to be full sentences, and he won't restrict us to just vocabulary lists, so I actually have to say stuff out loud."

Yesterday she had written "Tengo un perro," and today she had switched the word, and she wasn't sure why she'd done it. She said both versions under her breath, listening. Perro. Perra. One had an a at the end, like her own name did, and when she'd written about her mother she had used words ending in a too, and her father's words had ended in o. "She's a girl," Georgia said. "That's why I'm confused. I wrote perro first."

"El perro is a male dog," said Mr. Greco. "La perra is a female dog."

story:
Charles sat at the kitchen table with his mother's old laptop, which had survived three years of being dragged to school in his backpack and was, his dad said, more durable than anything else in the house. On the screen, his Scratch cat chased a mouse back and forth, but the score box in the corner kept showing numbers that made no sense: 7, then 12, then 30. He wanted this to be the first game he actually finished, the one he could show Britany on Monday instead of another half-built project abandoned like last month's maze.

He remembered the maze now, sitting frozen in his account, and wondered whether he had given up too early that time. Not this one. He opened the mouse sprite's script and read it block by block. When the cat touched the mouse, a block said change score by 1, and below it a forever loop spun the whole thing around again. That part looked right. So the mouse was earning points, and the cat was chasing it, but the number had never once started clean. He thought about what he could not see: somewhere, something was deciding what the score was worth before the game even began. He had a candidate for the culprit, and there was one way to test it.

He dragged in a green flag block, snapped a set score to 0 block under it, and clicked the flag. Zero. He touched the cat to the mouse once. One. He sat back so fast he nearly knocked over his water.

A message popped up from Donovan: "Your game is broken. I played it at recess on Britany's account and got 84 points before I even moved." Charles laughed, typed back "Fixed it. Made a variable called score, set it to 0 when the green flag is clicked, then change score by 1 for each point. Come over and lose properly," and hit send. Down the hall, his dad called that dinner was in ten minutes. Charles clicked the flag one more time, just to watch the zero appear.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A pet microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details.
story:
Wyatt stood at the front desk of the animal shelter, holding the adoption papers for a wiry terrier mix named Biscuit, when a woman rushed in with a muddy beagle draped in a beach towel. The dog was shivering and wore no collar at all. How did anyone know where a dog like that belonged?

Mr. Sato came out from the back room carrying a small handheld device that looked a bit like a chunky remote control. He waved it slowly over the beagle's shoulder blades, and it beeped. "There's a microchip in there," he said. Wyatt leaned closer. A microchip? He had pictured something like a dog tag, but this was inside the dog, invisible from the outside.

"How small is it?" Wyatt asked.

Mr. Sato held up his thumb and finger, barely apart. "About the size of a grain of rice. It doesn't hold an address or anything, just an ID number. The scanner reads the number, and we look it up in a registry to find the owner's contact details." He copied a string of digits off the scanner's screen and typed it into the shelter computer. Sure enough, a name and a phone number came up, and he called while the beagle gulped down water.

Wyatt turned the idea over while Biscuit sniffed his sneakers. A dog could lose every collar and tag in the world and still carry proof of who owned it, tucked under the skin where nobody could see. Was there a chip in Biscuit? The adoption paperwork was vague about it, just a line that said "chipped: yes" with no detail, so Wyatt decided to test it. "Could you scan him?" he asked.

Mr. Sato ran the wand over Biscuit's shoulders the same slow way, and Wyatt watched, holding his breath. The scanner stayed silent for a second, then chirped and flashed a number that was nothing like the beagle's. That was proof, real proof, printed right there. Wyatt copied it onto his adoption folder in careful pencil, thinking that tomorrow he would call the registry and check that the contact details were his family's and not some stranger's.

His friends Kianna and Cedar were waiting outside with the leash they had brought as a congratulations present, blue with little bones on it. "Guess what Biscuit has inside him," Wyatt said, and Biscuit trotted out the door, tail spinning like a propeller.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends

fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
story:
Grandpa's living room smelled like popcorn and old leather chairs, and every seat was taken. Anthony squeezed onto the rug between Anya and Thea while the screen showed the stadium filling up, thousands of fans waving towels. "Listen to that crowd," Grandpa said from his recliner. "That noise wins games. The home team feeds on it." The blitzing linebackers could hardly hear the quarterback, the announcer said, because it was so loud.

Anthony wasn't so sure. He remembered something he'd found a few weeks ago for a project and pulled it up on his tablet. In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1. Almost exactly even. No home advantage at all. "Grandpa," he said, holding up the screen, "look at this. In 2020, when almost nobody was in the stands, home teams went 127-128-1." Grandpa squinted at it. "That's barely under five hundred," Anya said, doing the math out loud. Thea leaned over. "So the cheering doesn't actually do it?" "It doesn't look like it," Anthony said.

Grandpa rubbed his chin. "Well, now. That's strange, because I retired in 2020 and watched every game that year on this very chair. Empty stadiums, cardboard people in the seats. Contemporary football, I called it, not like the games of my day." He paused. "And you know what? I never noticed any of that myself. The home teams played just fine." Anthony grinned. "So it's not the crowd. Maybe it's travel, or knowing the field, or something nobody can see." "Or maybe," Grandpa said, "football is just football."

Thea poked Anthony's arm. "Test it, then. Watch the whole game and count the false starts when it's loud." Anthony grabbed a notepad from the side table and wrote FALSE STARTS at the top. On screen, the quarterback barked the count, the crowd roared, and the visiting tackle jumped early. "That's one," Anthony said, and Grandpa laughed so hard his chair creaked. "Two can play at this," Grandpa said, reaching for his own pad from the drawer. "Loser does the dishes." On the wall above the TV hung Grandpa's old team photo, part of the family's sports heritage going back three generations, and Anthony thought his own page in that story was just getting started. The kickoff sailed into the lights, and both of them bent over their notepads, pencils ready.

story:
On Saturday morning Ethan's dad handed him a phone in a cracked cereal bowl, which was the family's idea of a ceremony. "Group chat's already set up," Dad said. "Your mom, your sister, me. Try not to text us anything before seven a.m."

Ethan spent the afternoon learning the phone. He figured out how to install a chess app, how to silence notifications, and how to send a photo to Jaida, who replied with a thumbs-up and the words "FINALLY." At 4:52 a text arrived from a number he didn't know. "GAME ACCOUNT ALERT: Your account will be deleted in 24 hours unless you verify your password now. Reply with password to keep your account." His stomach dropped, because he did have a game account, and he had just made a password for it that same day.

He typed his password, then stopped. He opened the family group chat. "If a company texts you and asks for your password, is that real?" His mom replied first with a single question mark. His sister wrote, "omg no." Then his dad called him from the garage, and Ethan walked over holding the phone out like evidence. They looked at the message together. Ethan noticed the sender address was a jumble of letters, not the game company's actual name, which appeared in his app. He remembered a poster in Mr. Santos's classroom, in the corner by the pencil sharpener, that he had never bothered to read. On Monday he went early and read it. Then he texted Jaida and Katherine at lunch: "It's called phishing. Somebody pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away your password or private information."

Katherine wrote back, "Wait, like fishing? With bait?" Ethan said basically. She asked if he'd fallen for it. He admitted he had typed the password but deleted it before sending. "The delete button is my best friend now," he said, and Jaida laughed so hard the lunch monitor looked over.

That evening Ethan reported to the group chat like an impartial referee delivering a verdict: "One fake message received. Zero passwords given away. Account not deleted. The company never asks for your password anyway." His sister replied with a GIF of a fish grabbing a hook and spitting it out. His dad wrote, "Good work. Now go look up whether the school's lunch menu is in some database you can check, because I want to know if it's pizza Friday." Ethan was already searching.

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: The one exception in standard guitar tuning is the G string, which is pressed at the fourth fret, not the fifth, to match the open B string.
story:
The church basement smelled of coffee and old hymnals, and the folding chairs had been pushed against the wall to make room for music stands. Isabella unzipped the case and lifted out the guitar Mr. Brown kept in the storage closet for kids who didn't own one. In three days the youth group was leading the Sunday songs, and she was the only one who could play more than three chords.

She had learned the tuning trick from Ellis at school: press a string at the fifth fret, and it should sound the same as the next thinner string played open. You started from the low E, worked your way up, and listened until the two notes melted into one. Penelope sat beside her with her eyes closed, because Penelope said she could hear the wobble between out-of-tune notes better than she could see anything.

Isabella pressed the low E at the fifth fret and plucked the A string. Wobble. She turned the tuning key a hair at a time, and Penelope raised a hand when the wobble turned into a smooth hum. They did the same for the D string, then the G, then the B, each time matching the fifth fret to the open string above it. Then Isabella strummed a G chord, the one they would need first on Sunday, and it sounded like a dropped pan.

"That's worse than when you started," Penelope said.

They tuned again, even more slowly, and the chord was still wrong. Isabella checked every string against the fifth fret below it, and everything matched. She was starting to think the guitar itself was broken, some barren dead spot in the wood that no amount of tuning could fix, when Mr. Brown came down with the coffee urn.

"Can you hear this?" she asked him, and played the chord.

Mr. Brown listened with his head tipped, then said, "Try your G string again. Check where you pressed it."

Isabella looked. She had matched the G at the fifth fret to the open B, the same as every other pair. She slid her finger down one fret, to the fourth, and plucked. The note landed square on the open B, no wobble at all. The G string was the one exception. She retuned it, strummed the chord, and the whole thing rang out clean and full, big enough to fill the room.

Penelope opened her eyes. "Do it again."

Isabella did it again, and this time she sang along.

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor

fact: Spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus or worsening pain around a cut can be signs of infection and a reason to see a doctor.
story:
Bently held out his arm like a knight surrendering a sword. "Fix me, Doctor Scarlett. I fell off the porch rail practicing my cool lean."

"My grandma charges a cookie tariff for lessons," Scarlett said, tearing open a bandage from the first aid tin. "One cookie per wound. House rules." Grandma, watching from her rocking chair, nodded solemnly, as if this were a law she had signed herself.

Scarlett pressed the pad over the scrape, wrapped the bandage snug but not tight, and checked that Bently could still wiggle his fingers. "Not too tight, or your hand turns purple and falls off," she said. "Probably." Bently wiggled his fingers extra fast, just in case. Grandma glanced at the clock and said, "Ten minutes, you two, or we miss the ferry to the fair. And Scarlett, since you're the expert now, look at this." She held out her hand. Two days ago she had sliced it on a can lid, and Scarlett had bandaged it herself, feeling very professional. Now the skin around the cut was red, and the redness had spread past the edges of the bandage like a stain growing on a shirt.

Scarlett touched the skin near it, careful and light. Warm. Hot, even. The whole area looked puffy and swollen, and when Grandma flexed her fingers she winced. "It hurts worse than yesterday," Grandma admitted. "And there's a bit of pus."

Scarlett stood very still, thinking. A cut was supposed to get better, not worse. Spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus, pain that got worse instead of better. All five. That was the whole checklist from the first aid book she'd read under the covers with a flashlight, and this cut had checked every single box. "Grandma," she said, "this needs a doctor. Not a bandage. A doctor."

Grandma sighed and resigned herself to missing the ferry, the fair, and the candy apples. "Well," she said, reaching for her keys, "suppose you'd better drive." Scarlett was already dialing the clinic, and Bently was wrapping the leftover bandage around the cat, who looked deeply offended.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: In a physical change, a substance changes its shape or state but stays the same substance, the way ice melting into water is still water.
story:
Violet stared at her tray of ice cubes, which were melting into a puddle faster than she had planned, and tried to draft her display board for the third time. Her poster read "The Great Change Test," and underneath she had taped two photos: her ice cubes, and a rusty old horseshoe from her grandfather's barn. The problem was the line she was supposed to write beneath them. She had guessed "both are changes," but that felt thin, and the judges would walk the rows in twenty minutes.

Mika leaned over from the next table, stretching a blob of bright green slime between her hands. "Mine is the elastic slime dynasty," she announced. "Three generations of slime recipes, perfected by me. Judges love a dynasty. Also I really want to beat Laurent, because he said my project was 'just toy stuff,' and I intend to make him eat those words with a spoon." She snapped the slime back into a ball. "So what's your actual question, Violet? What are you testing?"

"That's the thing," Violet said. "I melted ice and it turned to water. I watched it. And the horseshoe got all orange and flaky. They both changed, but they didn't feel like the same kind of change, and I can't say why without just saying 'they're different.'" She crouched down and peered at the puddle. "The water is still here. Nothing went anywhere." She dipped a finger in it, then looked at the horseshoe photo again. "But the rust... the iron didn't just move somewhere else. Something new is sitting on that shoe." She stood up so fast she knocked over a cup. "Wait. That's the test. If I freeze my puddle, I should get ice back. Same stuff, different shape. But I can't un-rust anything."

Mr. Suzuki, the judge with the clipboard, stopped at her table right then, which was terrible timing and also maybe perfect timing. "So, young scientist, what did you find out?"

Violet took a breath. "Melting ice is a physical change," she said. "The stuff changes its shape or its state, but it stays the same substance. Ice melting into water is still water. Rusting is the other kind, because it makes something new." She grabbed the cup she'd knocked over, now full of meltwater, and held it up. "I can freeze this and get ice cubes back. Nobody can turn a rusty horseshoe back into a shiny one just by cooling it."

Mr. Suzuki wrote something on his clipboard. Across the aisle, Laurent was quietly watching, arms crossed. Mika stretched her slime into a long green rope and let it hang between the two tables like a bridge.

"Ten out of ten for the freeze test," Mika whispered. "Laurent, your vinegar volcano is about to be extinct."

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: An "I-statement," such as "I feel left out when plans change," describes the speaker's own feelings instead of blaming, which makes the listener less likely to get defensive.
story:
Olivier had both friends in his garage, which was bad, because Cade and Dwayne were not speaking to each other. They stood on opposite sides of his dad's workbench like two cats guarding the same sunny spot. Cade had his arms crossed. Dwayne was kicking a paint can, gently, as if the paint can had done nothing wrong and he knew it.

"You always ditch me," Cade said. "Saturday, the skate park. You said you'd come, then you went with your cousin instead."

"That's not ditching, that's my cousin," Dwayne said, and the paint can rang like a dull bell. "And anyway, you never text me back, so why should I?"

Olivier raised both hands the way he had seen a referee do it in a soccer video. His problem was simple: he wanted his alliance of garage-cronies back, and he wanted it before Saturday, when all three of them had planned to build a ramp. If he took Cade's side, he'd lose Dwayne. If he took Dwayne's side, Cade would storm out and the ramp would be an impoverished, lonely pile of wood. He needed a third option.

Then he noticed something. Every sentence either of them said started with "you." You always. You never. You did. Each "you" made the other one's face contract into a deeper scowl, like a slug touching salt. Olivier had learned about this in Mr. Pierre's class, one sleepy Tuesday, and he had thought it was boring then. It was not boring now.

"New rule," he announced. "Nobody says a sentence starting with 'you.' You have to start with 'I' and say your own feeling. It's called an I-statement. Watch." He turned to Cade. "Say it again, but that way."

Cade rolled his eyes so hard it must have hurt. But he tried. "I feel left out when plans change."

Dwayne stopped kicking the paint can. His shoulders came down from around his ears. "Well," he said, "I feel bad that I didn't tell you about my cousin. I just forgot."

"Forgot," Cade repeated. "Okay. That's annoying, but it's not ditching."

"Bring your cousin Saturday," Olivier said quickly, before anyone could invent a new argument. "He can hold the wood."

Dwayne picked up the paint can and offered it to Cade like a trophy. "Peace offering. It's mostly dried up, but it's blue."

Cade took it. "Blue is literally the ramp color I wanted."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
story:
The campfire crackled in the ring of stones, and Xavier poked at it with a stick until a spiral of sparks rose into the dark. Across the fire, Jorge sat hunched with his arms crossed over his shoulders, which were blotchy red and shiny with aloe gel from the first-aid cabin.

"I put on sunscreen this morning," Jorge said, wincing as he leaned back. "Before we even went down to the lake. So how did this happen?"

Xavier thought about that while he turned his stick in the flames. Jorge had slathered on sunscreen at eight o'clock, that much was true. Then the whole cabin had spent the afternoon at the lake, swimming and racing each other along the shore and hauling the canoe. Xavier remembered the counselor calling out the time when they hiked back for dinner: nearly five. He counted on his fingers, and an insight slid into place. "Jorge, you put it on at eight and then stayed out until five. That's a really long time." He flipped the stick over. "And you were in the water all afternoon, too."

Anabel, who was roasting a marshmallow on the other side of the fire, looked up. "My mom says sunscreen wears off," she offered. "You have to put it on again every two hours when you're outside."

"And right after swimming," said Mr. Pham, the camp director, walking past with an armload of firewood. He only paused for a second before going on, but that was enough. Swimming, Xavier thought. That washes it right off. Nobody had reminded Jorge to reapply anything, all day, and so the morning coat had rubbed away hours before dinner.

"Tomorrow," Xavier said, "we set a rule. New sunscreen every two hours, even if we feel fine, and the second anybody climbs out of the lake." He glanced at Jorge's glowing shoulders. "And if somebody's shoulder looks like a stop sign, we restrict the afternoon swimming to the shady part of the shore until it heals."

"Deal," Jorge said, though he smiled like it cost him something. Anabel pressed her cold marshmallow gently against Jorge's arm, and he sighed with relief so dramatic that even Mr. Pham laughed from the woodpile.

"You know," Anabel said, waving her marshmallow like a tiny white flag, "that was almost eloquent, Xavier. Stop signs and shady shores. You should give the campfire speech every night."

"I'll take the job." Xavier fed his stick to the fire and watched the flames catch. "First speech starts now: everybody up, sunscreen meeting at the picnic table, eight sharp."

The box had been in Alexis's backpack all morning, and by the time the bus lurched out of the school parking lot, he could not wait any longer. He tore the tape off, lifted out the phone his parents had given him for his birthday, and held it where Abigail and Emerson could see over the seat. "First one I've ever had," he said. The bus rattled past the field where the track team ran laps, and Alexis remembered his coach saying his grades had to come before any scholarship talk, so the phone went into his pocket with the screen off. He would figure out the rest a little at a time. Abigail tapped his shoulder. "Text me when you get home," she said. "Your number's on the card in the box."
