story:
Grandpa's study smelled like old paper and pencil shavings, and the map spread across the desk was so big it hung over the edges onto a chair. "Find my hometown," Grandpa said, tapping a spot in the far north. "If you can tell me exactly where it is, we'll video call your cousin and you can read it to her yourself."

Matthew leaned over the map until his nose nearly touched the paper. Thin lines curved across it in every direction, some running sideways, some running up and down, and little numbers sat along the edges like tiny measurements. "This one," he said, pointing at a line labeled 49. "It's on the forty-ninth line."

"Latitude," Grandpa said. "The sideways ones are latitude. The up-and-down ones are longitude." He set a magnifying glass beside Matthew's elbow, then shuffled off to make tea, because his knees signaled rain was coming and he wanted to be seated when it arrived.

Matthew traced the line with one finger and found the little black dot of the hometown sitting just above it, close to where a longitude line crossed. So it was near 49 degrees latitude, and near some other number for longitude. He presumed that meant the numbers worked like street addresses, one telling you how far across, one telling you how far up. He checked another city, Toronto, and found it sitting near 43 degrees. Six degrees apart. Then he remembered something from Ms. Addo's class, written on the board while Tyler was trying to throw paper clips into Kenzi's hood: one degree of latitude covers about 111 kilometers, or about 69 miles, of north-south distance. He counted on his fingers. Six degrees. Six times 69 miles.

"Grandpa!" Matthew called. "Your hometown is about 414 miles north of Toronto. Six degrees times sixty-nine miles." He said it twice more while Grandpa settled into his chair with his tea, and then Matthew got out his notebook and wrote the location the way a real navigator might: close to 49 degrees north latitude, west longitude seventy-something, roughly 414 miles north of Toronto, or about 666 kilometers, since six times 111 was 666.

Grandpa squinted at the notebook, then at Matthew, and pulled out his phone. "Let's call your cousin and see if the boy is right." The call connected, and Grandpa held up the notebook without a word. On the screen, the cousin leaned close, then laughed. "He's got it," she announced, and behind her somebody shouted, "Unanimous!" Matthew grinned and drew a small star next to his numbers.

"Tomorrow," Grandpa said, tapping the map's vast blue ocean, "we find the shipwreck."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: Many Canadian municipalities let residents ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting, which is called appearing as a delegation.
story:
Alexis stood in the community centre kitchen with a stack of foam cups, listening to her grandmother describe the new bylaw. Anyone who wanted to sell baking at the Saturday farmers' market inside the centre now had to pay for a special licence, and her grandmother said forty dollars a season was too much for her lemon loaves.

"That's bizarre," Alexis said. "You've been selling here for six years." She turned a cup over in her hands, thinking. There had to be a way to change a rule that seemed wrong, and it wouldn't be by ignoring it, because then the market supervisor would just send her grandmother home.

At the front desk, she asked the receptionist who made bylaws. The answer was city council. Then Alexis found the council website on the lobby computer and read the rules for meetings. Her reflex was to look for an email address, but what she found instead was better: a page saying residents could ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting. Five minutes, the page said, and the request had to go in ahead of time. "It's called appearing as a delegation," Alexis read aloud, and copied the phrase onto her wrist with a pen.

That night at her grandmother's house, she practised. Forest came over with Savannah, and the three of them rearranged the kitchen chairs into a pretend council chamber. Mr. Lewandowski, the neighbour whose garden shared the fence, agreed to supervise the rehearsal and play the councillors. Alexis's first try was a disaster. She talked too fast, forgot her numbers, and stood twisting the corner of her note card until it went soggy.

"You have five minutes, so use them," Savannah said. "Slow down at the important part."

The second try was better. Alexis explained who she was, how long her grandmother had sold at the market, and that the licence fee would push out small sellers like her. She ended with a plain request: lower the fee for people who sell only a few weekends a season. Forest held up his phone timer and gave her a thumbs-up at four minutes and twelve seconds.

The real meeting came two weeks later. Alexis stood at the little wooden podium while the councillors watched from their raised desks, and she spoke about lemon loaves and forty dollars and Saturday mornings at the community centre. When she finished, one councillor leaned toward his microphone.

"That was a fine delegation," he said. "Let's look at that fee."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: StoryCorps is a project in which people record interviews with family members, and with permission the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress.
story:
Grandpa Whit had been sleeping in the guest bedroom for six days, and Hayden had one night left to solve the problem. The problem was this: Grandpa told the best stories in the world, about flooding creeks and runaway mules and a one-eyed schoolteacher, and when he drove home tomorrow, the stories would go with him.

Hayden had tried writing them down, but Grandpa talked faster than any pencil. He'd tried memorizing, which lasted about as long as ice cream in July. On Thursday afternoon he sat on the guest bed, chin in his hands, staring at the empty bookshelf like it might hand him an idea. The room felt almost desolate without Grandpa's suitcase exploding socks everywhere, though Grandpa himself was downstairs burning toast.

Then he remembered. Neve had recorded her grandmother last month for a school project, and she'd mentioned a website. He called her from the hallway. "That thing your grandma did," he said. "The recording thing."

"StoryCorps," Neve said. "You record an interview with a family member. They keep it, and with permission it gets saved at the Library of Congress. Like, the actual Library of Congress, in Washington."

"With my grandpa's voice? In a giant library?"

"On a shelf with a spine, probably," Neve said, "right next to a million other people's grandpas."

Hayden tried to evade the awkward part, but Neve sniffed it out anyway. "You have to ask permission, doofus. Grandparents love being asked."

That evening, Hayden borrowed his mom's phone, knocked on the guest bedroom door, and found Grandpa attempting to fold a shirt into something that resembled a dumpling. "Grandpa. One last story before you leave. But this time I record it."

Grandpa raised an eyebrow. "For whom? The FBI?"

"For the Library of Congress," Hayden said, and explained, all in a rush, how the recording could be saved there if Grandpa said yes. Grandpa went quiet, which was rare enough that a tumbleweed could have rolled through the room. Then he sat down on the bed like a man accepting a medal.

"You mean my mule story outlasts me?" he said. "Son, start recording before I remember how to be humble."

Hayden hit the red button. "Question one. The mule. Go."

"The mule," Grandpa began, "was named Biscuit, and he had the manners of a pirate."

The phone hummed on the nightstand, saving every word.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Pumice is an igneous rock full of gas bubbles trapped as lava cooled, and many pieces are light enough to float on water.
story:
Jace crouched by the fire pit at Camp Widow Creek, turning a gray chunk of rock over in his hands while his friend Greyson poked at a beetle with a stick. Their teacher, Ms. Ferreira, had promised a prize to whoever sorted the most rocks correctly into the three boxes she had labeled igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. Jace wanted that prize badly, mostly because it was a giant chocolate bar, and partly because Greyson kept saying his own pile would crush Jace's pile "by a huge percentage."

"That one's sedimentary," Greyson said, pointing at the rock in Jace's hand. "It's all layered, like a sandwich."

"It's not layered, it's bubbly," Jace said, holding it up. The whole surface was pitted with little holes, like a sponge that had given up. He dropped it into the igneous box anyway, because igneous meant rock from cooled lava, and lava seemed like the sort of thing that would bubble.

They hauled their finds down to the mess hall, where Nia was already waiting with a bucket of lake water she had dragged up the hill for reasons she refused to explain. "I wanted to wash my rocks," she said, as if that were normal, which for Nia it was. The hillside around camp was so barren of anything interesting that washing rocks counted as entertainment.

Jace set his bubbly gray rock on the table to sort his other finds, and Greyson, reaching past him for the bean dip, knocked it off the edge. It landed in Nia's bucket with a splash. "Sorry," Greyson said, and then they all froze, because the rock was not sinking. It sat on the water like a beach ball.

"It floats," Nia whispered. "Rocks don't float."

"This one does," Jace said. His brain started churning. A rock full of gas bubbles, trapped as lava cooled, that would be light, and light things could float. He remembered Ms. Ferreira saying the word at the start of the week: pumice. He grabbed the rock out of the bucket, dripping, and held it up. "It's pumice. It's igneous, from lava, and the bubbles got trapped in it. That's why it floats."

Ms. Ferreira came over, looked in the bucket, looked at the rock, and raised an eyebrow. "Five points for the igneous box," she said, "and five more for the floating demonstration."

Greyson groaned and slid his sandwich-layered rock toward the sedimentary box. "Fine. You win this round." He paused. "Compromise? We split the chocolate bar."

"Sixty-forty," Jace said, wringing out his sleeve. "My percentage."

Nia fished a pebble from the bucket and dropped it back in. It sank, plunk, and she grinned. "One out of two rocks floating is still better than I expected."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: A passphrase of several random words, like the 2011 xkcd comic's example 'correct horse battery staple', is long enough to be hard to guess yet easy to remember.
story:
Emily had ten minutes before the sleepover movie started, and her old password had just been rejected for the third time.

"That's the one you use everywhere," Elora said, spinning her desk chair around. "You told me. Your email, the game, everything."

"I know." Emily stared at the laptop on Elora's desk. A message had popped up on her favorite writing site: someone in another city had tried to log into her account. It hadn't worked, but the site wanted her to change her password anyway. "It's 'emily2013.' How did they even guess it?"

Elora shrugged. "People guess stuff like that. Want to install the password manager my sister uses? It remembers everything for you."

"Then it has to be one password that guards all the others, and I'd better not mess that one up." Emily pulled a sticky note toward her and started writing. "Okay. How about 'emily2013!'"

"You added one symbol. Come on."

Emily thought about the time she'd used the same password for her bike lock and her locker at school, back in fourth grade. Lena had guessed it in about a minute, and for a week everyone opened Emily's locker as a joke. Emily had laughed along, but she still remembered how her stomach had dropped. Maybe reusing passwords was the same mistake, just invisible.

She tried something new. She looked around the room for random words, ones that had nothing to do with her. "Elora, give me four words. Anything."

"Turtle. Cactus. Lemon. Piano."

Emily typed turtlecactuslemonpiano into the site's tester. "It says it would take forever to guess." She said it slowly, testing the idea. "Four random words. It's long enough that it's hard to guess, but it's easy for me to remember." She tried to picture a turtle balancing on a cactus, holding a lemon, playing a piano, and grinned. There was no way anyone could guess that.

"But you can't use it on your email too," Elora said. "Remember your locker."

"I know, I know." Emily started a second list, her pen moving fast. "Lena. Quick, I need four more words before the movie."

From down the hall, Lena's voice called, "Does 'purple donkey saxophone blizzard' work?"

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: A line with a positive slope rises as you read from left to right, while a line with a negative slope falls.
story:
Olivia slid her worksheet across the table so Lainey could see it. The problem said y = 2x + 3, and Mr. Henry wanted them to solve for y when x equaled four, then plot enough points to draw the whole line. Lainey, who wanted to beat Anastasia in the club's graphing race, had already drawn three lines and was halfway through a fourth.

"Try x equals one," Lainey said. "Then two. The points should correspond, one x to one y, like they match up."

Olivia calculated. When x was one, y came out to five. When x was two, y was seven. She plotted both points, then connected them with her ruler and sat back. Her line went up, climbing from the lower left toward the upper right.

"That's a positive slope," Lainey said, pointing. "A line with a positive slope rises as you read from left to right."

Olivia nodded, then flipped to the next problem: y = -2x + 3. She did the steps again. Two times x, then subtract, then add three. When x was one, y was one. When x was two, y was negative one. She plotted the points and drew the line, and this one went the other way, sliding downhill from the upper left down to the lower right.

"Mine falls," Olivia said. "Same numbers, but the minus sign flips it."

Anastasia leaned over from the next table. "I made a database of all the equations Mr. Henry ever gave us, so nobody has to guess which ones climb. But I put my name on every page, so much for staying anonymous."

"Nobody cares about your pages," Lainey said. "Race you on the last one."

Mr. Henry posted the final equation on the board: y = 3x minus 1. Olivia solved it, plotted two points, and checked which way her pencil would travel. She smiled and drew her line rising to the right.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
story:
The tryout list went up on Friday, and Elijah's name was not on it. He found out at school, but he did the real thinking at home, at the kitchen table, with a mug of cocoa going cold beside him.

Isabel had texted him the names of the fourteen kids who made the basketball team. Elijah read the message three times, then grabbed a pencil and retrieved the tryout sign-up sheet from his backpack. Next to each name he wrote the player's birthday, which he mostly knew because the coach had made everyone say it out loud on the first day. When he finished, he counted. Nine of the fourteen were born in January, February, or March. Only two had birthdays after September, and one of those was Milo, who was already the tallest kid in grade six.

He called Isabel. "Can I read you something?" He read his list of names and dates. "The kids born early in the year got picked more. All of them are months older than the December kids like me."

"That's a thing," Isabel said. "My cousin calls it the relative age effect. It happens in lots of sports."

Elijah had spent the weekend deciding he just wasn't good enough. Now he wasn't sure. He wrote a short email to Mr. MacLeod, who coached the team: "I noticed most of the players picked were born early in the year, and studies have found that happens a lot in youth sports. I'd like to try again. Could I come to one practice and show you?" He reread it, deleted the last sentence because it sounded turbulent and demanding, and sent it anyway.

Monday evening, Mr. MacLeod called the house. "Come Wednesday," he said. "Bring your shoes." Elijah packed his bag that night, set it by the door, and shot free throws at the driveway hoop until the porch light came on.

At Wednesday's practice he scored twice, once on a pass from Milo, who grinned at him across the turbulent cluster of bodies under the net.

"After this," Elijah panted, "I'm going to be like a January kid."

"You already play like one," Milo said.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own path to the battery, so the others stay lit if one bulb breaks.
story:
The skate park at dusk smelled like warm rubber and sunscreen, and Autumn spread her science project across the picnic table by the half-pipe. Her battery, switch, and three small bulbs sat in a careful row, waiting to become the light display she had promised Mr. Lim, the caretaker who had said she could set it up for Friday night practice. He had even gone to the office to authorize it, coming back with a signed note that said one line: Autumn's lights, one table, one night.

"It worked at home," Autumn said, clipping the last wire. Mia skated over, wheels rattling the concrete, and Matilda trailed behind with the screwdriver in her back pocket like a tail. Autumn flipped the switch. All three bulbs glowed.

Then Mia leaned in to look closer, knocked the middle bulb with her elbow, and it flickered and died. The other two went dark too. The table went black except for the last molten orange streak of sunset behind the ramp.

"Great," Matilda said. "One dead bulb, zero lights."

Autumn stared at the wires. Last month she had done this same thing on a school project, wiring every bulb in one chain, and when one failed she had panicked, torn it apart, and taken a lower mark rather than trying to fix it. She still wasn't sure whether she had been lazy that day or just scared. She thought about it while Mia fanned herself with the signed note.

"Each bulb has its own path to the battery," Autumn said slowly, following the wires with her finger. "That's how I should build it. Then if one breaks, the others stay lit, because they aren't sharing its path."

"Are you sure?" Mia asked.

"Mostly. Let's find out." She unclipped the wires and rewired them, giving each bulb its own connection, the way the rivers near her grandmother's house split and ran side by side. Matilda handed her the screwdriver without being asked. It took three tries and one bent clip, and Autumn tried not to think about her bias toward quitting when something had already failed once, the way she assumed a broken thing stayed broken.

She flipped the switch. Two bulbs lit. She reached over, unscrewed one of them, and the other kept glowing, steady and small against the coming dark.

"Try it," Autumn said, holding out the dead bulb to Mia. "Break something."

Mia grinned and gave the middle bulb a deliberate tap with her knuckle. The light beside it never even blinked.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Reflected light is light bouncing back from the table onto a sphere's shadow side; it is lighter than the core shadow but always darker than the lit side.
story:
Alexis set his pencil down and stared at the lumpy circle on his sketchpad. Across the picnic table, Amelie was already darkening the shadow under her sphere, and Ms. Hughes had said the art show opened in exactly one hour. "Yours looks flat," Amelie said, not unkindly. "Mine looked flat too, until Elin helped me."

Elin leaned over from the next bench. "You put your light where?" she asked. Alexis pointed at the upper left of his drawing. "Okay, so the darkest part goes on the opposite side, and then you shade lighter and lighter toward the light. There's a bright spot, the highlight, right where the lamp hits it."

Alexis adjusted his grip on the pencil and tried again. He curved his strokes around the sphere instead of scribbling straight across, and slowly the circle began to bulge off the page. Then Elin held up her own drawing, and Alexis noticed something strange about it. The bottom edge of her sphere, on the shadow side, was almost white. It looked like two separate lamps were shining on it from opposite directions.

"That's not right," Alexis said slowly. "The lamp's only on one side. Why would the bottom of the shadow side be that bright?" He looked over at the still life on the table, a real ball under a real lamp, and squinted at its dark side. The very bottom edge wasn't pure black. It was lighter than the middle of the shadow, but nowhere near as light as the lit side. He tested the idea on his own paper, keeping that lower edge a middle gray, darker than anything on the lit half but lighter than the deepest shadow.

"Reflected light," Elin said, peering at the real ball. "Light bouncing back from the table onto the shadow side. I made mine too bright."

"You both have ten minutes," Ms. Hughes called from the craft cabin, where she was taping drawings to the wall.

Alexis shaded fast, keeping every part of the shadow side distinct from the lit side, dark against light. Amelie nudged his elbow. "Hang it up before you smudge it." He carried the pad across the grass and Ms. Hughes pinned it beside Elin's, sphere and shadow side by side under the tent.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
story:
Mia folded the newspaper page one more time and put it in her jacket pocket before Kate's mom drove them to the cemetery. The page had come out of the stack her father saved from two weeks ago, back when Grandma June first died. Mia had read it so many times she could almost say it from memory, but she still didn't understand one part.

At the cemetery, Kate and Marylou waited by the gate with flowers, and behind them Mr. Haile, the neighbor who used to fix Grandma June's fence, stood with his hat in his hands. The grass in the middle of the hill had been mowed, but the rows near the back were still long, so everyone walked carefully between the stones.

"There's something I have to check," Mia said, and she pulled out the page. "The obituary. It says she 'spent four years at sea with the merchant fleet.'" She looked at Mr. Haile. "Grandma never told me that. Not once. I thought maybe it was a mistake."

Mr. Haile smiled. "An obituary? That's the notice they publish when someone dies, with a short account of their life. Family, work, interests. She wouldn't have left her sailing out of it by accident."

Mia hadn't known that word before she found the page. Now she understood what it meant: whoever wrote it was supposed to tell the whole life, not just the parts people knew. She thought of all those afternoons dismantling old radios with Grandma on the porch, every part laid out on a towel and named. Grandma had named everything. Why not that?

Mia tried an experiment. "Mr. Haile, do you remember her ever talking about water?"

"Every time it rained," he said. "She'd say the deck rolled like the median of a busy road, cars going both ways. Never made sense to me till now."

It was ironic, Mia thought, that she had spent four years eating dinner across from a sailor and never once asked the right question. She knelt, set the folded page under the flowers, and smoothed it flat with both hands.

"Four years at sea," she said out loud. "Next time I visit, I'm bringing a map so you can show me where."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: If milk costs 2.65 and you pay with 5.00, the correct change is 2.35, whatever the currency.
story:
Sara's mother thrust a five-dollar bill into her hand at the front door. "We need milk before Grandma gets here at six, and I have to watch the soup. You're eleven now. You can do this." The clock on the microwave said 5:32. Sara looked at the bill, then at the door, then at the bill again. She had walked to the corner store before, but always with her mother, always with someone else holding the money.

She counted the steps down the front walk, because counting made her feel like she knew what she was doing. Twenty-one steps to the sidewalk. At the store, the cold air hit her face when she pushed through the door, and she found the milk cooler right where she remembered it. The sticker on the carton said 2.65. She carried it to the counter and handed over the five, and while the cashier rang it up, Sara did the arithmetic in her head, slowly, like walking downstairs in the dark. Five dollars take away two sixty-five. Two dollars and thirty-five cents. That was the change she should get.

The cashier handed her two coins and a bill. "Thanks, hon." Sara stepped aside so the man behind her could pay for his lottery tickets, and only then did she look at what was in her palm. Two dollars and five cents. A quarter was missing. Her stomach did a small flip. Was she sure? She checked the milk sticker again through the plastic bag: 2.65, plain as anything. And five take away two sixty-five was still 2.35, no matter how many times she said it to herself.

The line had grown, and the clock behind the counter said 5:41. Grandma arrived at six. Sara thought about just going home, but a missing quarter meant either she was wrong or the cashier was wrong, and she wanted to know which. Her friend Gerald had once told her that being assertive just meant saying what you needed without apologizing for it, and Sara had liked that word so much she'd written it on her arm with a pen. She took a breath and stepped back to the counter.

"Excuse me," she said, louder than she meant to. "The milk was two sixty-five, and I paid with five dollars, so the change should be two thirty-five. You gave me two oh five." The cashier looked at the register, then at her, then counted the coins in her palm with one finger. "Well, would you look at that. You're right, hon." He dropped a quarter into her hand.

Sara walked home grinning at the sky. It struck her as a kind of irony that the smallest coin had made her feel the tallest, and she wondered what other invisible arithmetic was hiding in ordinary afternoons, waiting for someone to count it out. She pushed through the front door and set the milk on the counter. "Two thirty-five," she told her mother, "and I counted every cent."

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: The Moon makes no light of its own; it shines only because it reflects sunlight.
story:
Alice had always thought the Moon glowed the way a lightbulb does, like it was burning something, and that was exactly what she planned to tell Aubree when she came over. Grandpa's lamp stood in the middle of the darkened den, its shade removed, blazing like a small sun. Alice held an orange ball at arm's length, ready to orbit it.

"Wait," Aubree said, dropping her backpack by the door. "What's all this?"

"Grandpa says if we mess up his den, we restore it with time and leisure after. Sit down and watch." Alice walked the ball slowly around the lamp, keeping her head still, like Earth. Halfway around, the ball's lit side faced away from her. She turned her head carefully, the way Grandpa had shown her, and gasped. "Aubree, look. I can only see the skinny lit edge. That's a crescent."

Aubree leaned in, agile on her knees, circling to see from Alice's viewpoint. "So it's the same ball the whole time?"

"It has to be. It's just..." Alice stopped, frowning. She moved the ball back to the start, where its whole lit face blazed toward her, then walked it half the orbit again and watched the light shrink to a sliver. "The lamp didn't change. The ball didn't change. The only thing that changed was where I was standing." Her voice went quick with excitement. "The Moon makes no light of its own. It shines only because it reflects sunlight. So the shape we see is just how much of the lit part is facing us."

From the doorway, Ms. Sokolov, who had come to return Grandpa's garden shears, clapped once. "Then show me a new moon," she said.

Alice carried the ball to the far side of the lamp, directly opposite herself, and the bright face turned completely away. The ball concealed its light behind its own dark side, a round shadow against nothing. "It's still there," she whispered. "We just can't see it."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A conclusion restates the thesis in fresh words and sums up the main points, but it should not introduce a brand-new argument.
story:
Eve slid her draft across the library table until it touched Paula's elbow. "Read the last part first," she whispered. Around them the afternoon crowd murmured, and Mr. Kaur was restacking the returns cart by the window. The three friends had until closing time to finish their essays for the display case by the front desk, where the best one would hang for a whole month with the writer's name in gold letters.

Eve was arguing that the school cafeteria should keep prices low even when inflation pushed them up. She had three solid paragraphs, but her favorite idea, a plan where students could trade cafeteria credits for fresh fruit from the community garden, had arrived late, scrawled into the final paragraph like a guest showing up after the party ended. Paula read it twice, chewing her pencil. "The fruit idea is your best one," she said, "but it shows up at the end like a surprise. It kind of knocks the rest over."

Enoch leaned over from his seat, his own essay about later library hours spread in front of him. "Mr. Kaur has a whole shelf on essays," he said. "The orange binder. I looked at it yesterday." He fetchedit, and Eve flipped through until she found the page on endings. The rule sat there in plain print: a conclusion restates the thesis in fresh words and sums up the main points, but it should not introduce a brand-new argument. She read it twice, then frowned at her own paper.

"So the ending is supposed to echo the beginning, not announce something new," she said slowly. "That means my garden idea isn't a conclusion. It's a whole main point that got born in the wrong place." She felt almost annoyed with the rule, because the idea had seemed so perfect right there, glowing at the bottom of the page. But then she began to see how it worked. She tested it on Enoch. "Listen to my intro. Cafeteria prices should stay low. Listen to my ending. Cafeteria prices should stay low, and here's why the garden makes that possible." Enoch nodded. "The second one sounds bigger," he said, "but it's actually two papers glued together."

Eve got to work. She lifted the garden idea out of the last paragraph and gave it a home of its own as her third main point, then adjusted her introduction so the reader would expect it. For her conclusion she found fresh words: instead of repeating "prices should stay low," she wrote that every student deserved a lunch that did not cost more each year. It summed up prices, the budget, and the garden without dragging in anything new. Paula read it and gave a thumbs-up so wide her elastic sleeve slipped down over her hand.

At the desk, Mr. Kaur accepted the pages with both hands, the way he took everything, as if each returned book were a small treasure. Eve watched him clip her essay to the top of the stack. "May I borrow that orange binder over the weekend?" she asked. "I'm going to need it again." He picked out the green-cap stick, paid the cashier, and marched home to test it.

The next morning he swiped the deodorant on, pulled on the same hoodie he had worn all week, and went to school. Parker sniffed near him in science and said, "Still wet dog, Cooper." Cooper's ears went hot. He had used the product. Something did not add up.

At lunch he laid out the evidence on the table like a detective. Monday he had worn the hoodie and smelled. Tuesday the same hoodie, plus deodorant, and still smelled. The armpit theory was biased, he realized, because he had only ever blamed his armpits and never checked anything else. Aleena leaned over his shoulder and read his notes. She pointed at his sleeve. "That thing is a hull of old sweat."

Cooper ran an experiment that evening. He showered, put on a completely fresh shirt and fresh socks, and left the hoodie on his desk. In the morning he sniffed the hoodie first. It smelled like a locker room floor. Then he smelled his clean shirt. Nothing. His armpits had not been the main suspects after all.

The deodorant went in his backpack anyway. He wore the clean shirt to school, and in science Parker leaned over, sniffed twice, and frowned. "Huh," Parker said. "What brand is that?" Cooper held up the green cap. "It's not the brand," he said. "Wash your hoodie tonight and find out."

Declan discovered the pimple on Tuesday morning, right in the middle of his chin, and school photos were on Friday. In the waiting room, the fluorescent lights seemed to shine directly on his chin, like a spotlight no one else had to stand in. On the wall beside the fish tank hung a poster about a clinic that helped refugee families get dental care, and Declan stared at it because it was easier than staring at his own reflection in the tank glass.

Viktor was in the waiting room too, because their appointments had been booked back to back. "What's wrong with your face?" Viktor asked, which was Viktor's way of saying hello. "School photos are Friday," Declan said. "And this showed up overnight. I didn't do anything. I ate the same dinner as always." Viktor leaned back in his chair. "My brother gets those. He says it's the sebum. Hormones during puberty make your skin's oil glands produce more oil, and it's called sebum, and it clogs your pores. That's what makes the pimples." Declan frowned. "Glands I can't see, making oil I can't see, causing a pimple I can definitely see." Viktor shrugged. "That's what he said."

When Ms. Dela Cruz came out to call him back, she looked at his chart, not his chin. She counted his teeth, praised his flossing, and asked about snacks. On the way out, Declan stopped by the front desk where they sold travel-size toothpaste. He checked his remaining allowance, then decided to prioritize a face wash and deodorant over the fancy toothpaste, because his old tube still had some left. His parents had been suggesting daily showers for weeks anyway, and now he had a reason that made sense to him.

That night he washed his face carefully, twice, and again in the morning. By Thursday the pimple was smaller, still there but dormant, like a volcano that had decided to go back to sleep. On Friday morning Devon saw him in the hallway and said, "Hey, your chin looks normal." Declan touched the spot once, lightly, and said, "Photos are fifth period.
